# On Noticing

There is a particular kind of attention that gets lost somewhere between childhood and whatever comes after it. A child can spend twenty minutes examining a beetle crossing a sidewalk crack, can find in a puddle a complete universe of oil-slick rainbows and drowned ants, can ask "why" seven times in a row about the color of the sky until the asking itself becomes the point rather than the answer. Somewhere along the way, most of us trade this kind of noticing for efficiency. We learn to see categories instead of things: *that's a bug, that's a puddle, that's the sky, move along.* The world becomes a set of labels we've already attached, and attaching them lets us stop looking.

I think about this trade-off a lot, mostly because I'm not sure it was a fair one. Efficiency is useful—nobody wants to re-derive the wheel every morning, and a life spent in perpetual beetle-watching would never get the laundry done. But there's a cost to the speed, and the cost is paid in texture. The world flattens. Days start to resemble each other not because they actually do, but because we've stopped checking.

I notice this most when I travel somewhere unfamiliar. Suddenly the labels don't work anymore. The street signs are in a language I can half-guess at, the food has textures I haven't catalogued, the light falls at an angle my body doesn't recognize as "afternoon" or "evening." And for a few days, everything is interesting again, not because the place is objectively more interesting than home, but because I haven't yet built the shortcuts that let me stop looking at it. Then, inevitably, the shortcuts arrive. By day five I know which street the bakery is on and I stop seeing the bakery.

This isn't a complaint, exactly. Shortcuts are how we function. But I think there's a kind of discipline—maybe even a kind of ethics—in trying to keep some part of your attention unautomated. Not all of it; that would be exhausting and probably a symptom of something. But some small percentage, held in reserve, devoted to looking at things as if you'd never seen them before, even things you've seen ten thousand times. The same coffee cup. The same tree outside the same window. The same person's face across the same table, which is maybe the most important one, because faces are exactly the kind of thing we stop looking at once we think we know them. We start reacting to our *memory* of the person instead of the person actually in front of us, updated by sleep or sadness or a new haircut or just the seven years that have passed since we really checked.

There's a story—I don't know if it's true, but it doesn't need to be—about a painter who was asked how long it took to paint a particular portrait. He said something like: forty years and ten minutes. Forty years of learning to see, and ten minutes of putting the paint down. I like this because it suggests that noticing isn't passive. It's not just opening your eyes and letting light hit your retina. It's a skill, trainable, the way a sommelier trains to taste apricot and wet stone in a glass of wine that would taste to me like "wine." The sommelier isn't pretending to taste more; they actually do, because they've spent years building the vocabulary and attention required to separate one sensation from another. Most of us are walking around with an undifferentiated wine-glass version of reality: vague, serviceable, mostly beige.

Language plays a strange double role here. On one hand, it's the thing that lets us flatten the world into categories in the first place—the word "tree" erases ten thousand actual, particular trees into one interchangeable concept. On the other hand, more precise language can do the opposite: it can force you to look closer. If you only have the word "tree," you'll only ever see a tree. If you learn the words for bark texture, leaf margin, the way certain species hold their branches at characteristic angles, you start seeing oaks and lindens and a particular gnarled maple that's been struck by lightning twice, instead of an undifferentiated green blur called "trees." Vocabulary, in this sense, is a kind of prosthetic for attention. The more words you have, the more distinctions you're capable of making, and the more distinctions you make, the more the world seems to expand rather than contract, even though it hasn't actually changed at all. Only your resolution has.

I wonder sometimes if this is what people mean when they talk about presence, or mindfulness, or whatever word currently has the least amount of irony attached to it. Not some mystical erasure of thought, but something closer to a refusal to let the labels do all the work. A willingness to recheck your assumptions about the cup, the tree, the face, the street—to ask, even briefly, *is this actually what I think it is, or is this just what I decided it was the last time I looked?*

The beetle on the sidewalk doesn't know it's a beetle. It doesn't know it's crossing a crack, or that the crack is in concrete, or that concrete is a human invention barely a few thousand years old, layered over dirt that's been there since before there were sidewalks or humans or words for either. It's just doing what it's doing, fully, without the mediating fog of categories. I'm not arguing we should all try to think like beetles—we can't, and wouldn't want to, since beetles presumably don't get to enjoy poetry or correctly assembled furniture. But there's something in that pure absorption worth stealing back, in small doses, on purpose, before the whole world quietly turns into wallpaper.
